title: The list you buy from
summary: Buying in Supermarket Simulator is done from lists rather than shelves: the game keeps sales items and a sales type, gives every row a UI element of its own, and lets the list be filtered and a product toggled before it goes through a product viewer.
body: What you can buy arrives as a list rather than as a room full of things. The game keeps sales items and a kind of sale of its own, which is how ordering stock, equipment and fittings can share one way of being shown.
Every row is a thing of its own in the interface. There is a UI element for a sales row, so a line in the list can be drawn, selected and changed without the list being rebuilt around it.
The list can be filtered. There are filter types and filtered items, and even a filter type for a toolbox, which is why the same catalogue can be narrowed to what you actually came for.
What the list shows goes through a product viewer, so the catalogue reads its products from a place of its own rather than each row holding a copy.
A row is not only a label. There is an item that toggles a product, which is how the list can turn something on or off rather than only describing it.
Furniture rows carry more than a name: there is a display colour and a dropdown item belonging to them, which is how a fitting can be chosen in a colour from the same list.

The game draws the rows with icons of its own. It ships item icons and separate sets for the things that are not products, which is why a bucket of paint and a floor look like catalogue entries rather than like photographs.
The image beside this entry is the game's own: the icon it uses for an item in that list.
What this entry does not tell you: how many items the list holds, how its sorting works, or what anything costs. We have not verified those numbers, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: What can be bought is kept as sales items with a kind of sale of its own.
Every row in the list is a UI element of its own.
The list can be filtered, with filter types and filtered items, including one for a toolbox.
What the list shows goes through a product viewer.
A row can toggle a product rather than only describing it.
Furniture rows carry a display colour and a dropdown item of their own.
